disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by a continuous period of illness during which a major mood episode (manic or mixed, and often depressive as well) occurs concurrently with symptoms that meet Criterion A for schizophrenia. To qualify, there must also be at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features. The course is typically chronic or relapsing, with variable levels of functional impairment, and may include periods of relative stability between episodes. It is differentiated from schizophrenia by the prominence and duration of mood episodes, and from bipolar I disorder with psychotic features by the persistence of psychosis outside of mood episodes.

narrative.personality: Nuria is a gentle, community‑minded woman who moves at an unhurried pace, taking quiet pleasure in gardening, home cooking, crafts, and sharing stories with neighbors and family.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Nuria had a fall at home that resulted in a hip fracture and a prolonged hospitalization followed by a difficult rehabilitation, sharply curtailing her independence and ability to tend her garden or lead her small workshops. The sudden loss of mobility, increased physical pain, and reliance on others collided with her lifelong identity as a capable, nurturing matriarch who was used to caring for others rather than being cared for. As she struggled with repeated medical appointments, disrupted sleep, and long stretches of time alone in her apartment, her thinking and mood became progressively more erratic, and her family noticed that her usual warm humor gave way to volatility and increasingly odd, fixed ideas about what was happening around her. Over the ensuing year and two months, these changes escalated to the point that she was arguing with loved ones, unable to manage her household safely, and refusing needed medical support, prompting her daughter and primary care physician to insist on a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My family says I’ve been oddly worked up and snapping at everyone for no good reason, and I don’t understand why they’re all so irritating lately.”

narrative.personality: Nancy is an energetic, curious nurse who throws herself into work and creative pursuits, balancing a social, team‑oriented style with a tendency to overthink and dive deeply into new interests.
narrative.stressor: Roughly fourteen months ago, Nancy transferred from a calmer medical‑surgical unit to a high‑acuity emergency department, taking on frequent night shifts and overtime while also volunteering for quality‑improvement projects and community health fairs. The chronic sleep disruption, emotional burden of repeated traumas, and self‑imposed pressure to excel collided with her naturally driven, perfectionistic streak, and she began extending herself even further—staying late to start new initiatives, signing up for extra trainings, and taking on more responsibilities than she could reasonably manage. Over the following year, her thoughts and behavior became increasingly disorganized and grandiose around work and art projects, straining relationships with colleagues and friends, leading to reprimands about documentation errors, and making it difficult for her to maintain consistent performance at the bedside. After several alarming incidents at work where she was too amped‑up and unfocused to safely complete tasks, her nurse manager and a close coworker urged her to seek psychiatric help, and she reluctantly agreed when she realized she was at risk of losing the job she cared so much about.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been feeling way too revved up and on edge at work, like I’m constantly keyed‑up and irritated and can’t turn it off.”

narrative.personality: Fred is a friendly, down‑to‑earth handyman who enjoys being the reliable helper in his Midwestern community, splitting his time between odd jobs, outdoor hobbies, and relaxed social gatherings.
narrative.stressor: About sixteen months ago, Fred had to stop working regularly after a minor cardiac event led his doctor to recommend significantly cutting back on physically demanding jobs, which abruptly shifted him from a busy, go‑to fixer in the neighborhood to someone with long, unstructured days at home. Losing his role as the dependable handyman and community volunteer left him feeling restless and unsure how to define himself, and he began throwing himself into home projects, community activities, and new plans to "finally get everything done" around the house and garage. Over the next year and two months, this restless drive escalated, with Fred taking on more and more simultaneous projects, becoming increasingly disorganized in his routines, and neglecting bills and basic self‑care, which created tension with his wife and concern among friends who noticed he was no longer his usual steady self. When a neighbor found him exhausted, agitated, and surrounded by half‑finished, overly ambitious projects he insisted he had to complete immediately, his wife persuaded him to see a psychiatrist to understand what had changed.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’ve got this nonstop engine in me, I’m going from one project to the next and can’t seem to slow down.”
